items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Dana sprinted toward the bus stop, but the doors hissed shut and the bus pulled away without her. She stood there for a moment, then squared her shoulders. The library was only six blocks the other way, and the science fair entry forms were due there by noon. She had been planning to drop them at school, but school was now impossible to reach in time. Dana started walking fast toward the library instead, rehearsing what she would say if the librarian told her the deadline had already passed.

Explain how Dana's missing the bus leads to her next decision, and how that choice moves the story toward its ending.
items.answer: Missing the bus removes Dana's original plan to turn in the forms at school, so the missed bus is the cause that forces a new choice. In response, she decides to walk to the library instead, which is still open and still able to accept the forms before noon. This choice moves the story toward its ending because it sends Dana toward the place where the deadline can still be met, setting up the final question of whether she will make it in time. The causal link is that the missed bus closes one path and pushes her to choose a second path that drives the plot toward its resolution.

steps: Identify the first episode: Dana misses the bus, which cancels her plan to drop the forms at school.
Identify the effect: because the school route is now impossible, she must find another way to meet the noon deadline.
Trace the decision that follows: she chooses to walk to the library, the one place that can still accept the forms.

Explain the link to the ending: the new choice sends her toward the deadline location, setting up whether she will make it in time. The answer must name the causal connection, not just retell the events.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The recital hall went dark in the middle of Marcus's piano piece. A few people gasped. Marcus's hands froze above the keys for one second. Then, instead of stopping, he kept playing in the dark, finding the notes by feel. He had practiced this piece so many times that his fingers knew the way without his eyes. When the lights flickered back on, he was three measures further along and had not missed a note. The audience, surprised, broke into applause before he had even finished.

Describe how Marcus reacts when the lights go out, and explain what his reaction reveals about him.
items.answer: When the lights go out, Marcus freezes for only a second and then keeps playing in the dark, finding the notes by feel. His reaction reveals that he is calm under pressure and deeply prepared. Because he has practiced the piece so many times, his fingers know it without his eyes, so he is able to continue rather than panic. His choice to keep going instead of stopping shows confidence and composure. The trait is supported by the text directly: he does not miss a note and even moves three measures ahead, which shows that his steadiness comes from real preparation rather than luck.

steps: Find the moment in the text: the hall goes dark during his performance.
Cite his specific response: he freezes for one second, then keeps playing by feel instead of stopping.
Infer the trait behind the action: calm, composure, and being well prepared, since his fingers know the piece without his eyes.
Anchor the trait in evidence so it is not an unsupported guess: he misses no notes and gains three measures, proving the steadiness comes from practice.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The campers had planned to hike to the ridge and camp there overnight. But by afternoon the sky in the west had turned a bruised gray, and the wind picked up cold and sudden. Their counselor checked the clouds, then the map. 'The ridge has no cover,' she said. 'If that storm reaches us up there, we have nowhere to go.' The group turned around and hiked back down to the sheltered valley camp instead, setting up their tents under the thick pines just as the first heavy drops began to fall.

Explain how the setting, specifically the coming storm, changes what the campers decide to do.
items.answer: The coming storm changes the campers' decision by making their original plan dangerous. They had planned to camp on the ridge, but the ridge has no cover, so a storm there would leave them exposed with nowhere to go. The setting, the approaching storm combined with the open, shelterless ridge, forces them to choose safety over their plan. As a result, they turn around and hike down to the sheltered valley camp under the thick pines. The link is direct: the weather and the lack of cover on the ridge cause the campers to abandon their plan and seek shelter, which is how the setting shapes the plot's events.

steps: Identify the setting detail that matters: a storm is approaching, and the ridge has no cover.
Connect that detail to the conflict: camping on the exposed ridge in a storm would be dangerous.
Trace the decision the setting forces: the group abandons the ridge plan and heads to the sheltered valley.
State the cause-and-effect link clearly, rather than just mentioning that a storm exists in the background.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

When the new student, Theo, joined the class in October, Jaylen rolled his eyes. Theo answered every question, raised his hand for every task, and Jaylen decided he was a show-off. For weeks Jaylen ignored him. Then the class was paired for a project, and Jaylen got Theo. Working together, Jaylen noticed that Theo answered so often because he was nervous about being new and wanted to prove he belonged. By the end of the project, Jaylen was saving Theo a seat at lunch.

Describe how Jaylen changes from the beginning of the passage to the end, and identify the event that caused the change.
items.answer: At the beginning, Jaylen dislikes Theo and judges him as a show-off, so he ignores him for weeks. By the end, Jaylen has changed: he saves Theo a seat at lunch, which shows acceptance and even friendship. The event that caused the change is being paired with Theo for the project. Working closely with him, Jaylen realizes that Theo answers questions so often because he is nervous and wants to prove he belongs, not because he is showing off. This new understanding, gained through the project, is the turning point that shifts Jaylen from judgment to friendship. The change is rooted in the specific event of working together, not in any earlier moment.

steps: Describe Jaylen at the start: he judges Theo as a show-off and ignores him.
Describe Jaylen at the end: he saves Theo a seat at lunch, showing acceptance.
Locate the turning-point event: being paired with Theo for the project.
Explain why that event caused the change: working together lets Jaylen see Theo's nervousness, which corrects his earlier judgment. Avoid blaming an earlier, unrelated moment.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

First, Nadia found the wounded sparrow on the sidewalk and carried it home in her cupped hands. Next, she made a small nest from a shoebox and an old scarf and fed the bird from an eyedropper for nine days. Then, one morning, the sparrow flew up to the windowsill and sat there, testing its wings. Finally, Nadia opened the window. The bird hesitated, hopped once, and flew out over the rooftops.

Put the four key events in the order they happen in the story, and explain which event comes immediately after Nadia feeds the bird for nine days.
items.answer: The four key events in order are: (1) Nadia finds the wounded sparrow on the sidewalk and carries it home; (2) she makes a nest and feeds the bird from an eyedropper for nine days; (3) the sparrow flies up to the windowsill and tests its wings; (4) Nadia opens the window and the bird flies out over the rooftops. The event that comes immediately after Nadia feeds the bird for nine days is the sparrow flying up to the windowsill to test its wings. The text signals this order with the words first, next, then, and finally, so feeding the bird leads directly to the bird recovering enough to perch and test its wings.

steps: Use the time-order signal words in the text: first, next, then, finally.
Match each signal word to its event to build the correct sequence.
Locate the event right after the nine days of feeding: the sparrow flies to the windowsill and tests its wings.
Confirm the order follows the story's chronology, not the order details happen to appear in any one sentence.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The coastal town had always relied on its lighthouse. Every night the keeper, old Mr. Reyes, climbed the spiral stairs and lit the great lamp so the fishing boats could find their way home. One autumn the storms grew fierce, and one night the lamp would not light. Mr. Reyes worked for an hour in the dark, freezing, his hands shaking. Out on the water, the boats circled, lost. Finally he remembered the spare oil in the cellar, ran down, fetched it, and got the lamp burning just as the first boat drifted dangerously close to the rocks.

Identify which stage of the plot the moment when 'the lamp would not light' represents, and explain your choice.
items.answer: The moment when the lamp would not light represents the rising action, the part of the plot where the central conflict appears and tension begins to build. It is not the resolution, because the problem is not yet solved, and it is not the climax, because the most intense moment comes later when Mr. Reyes races to get the lamp burning just as a boat nears the rocks. The failed lamp introduces the conflict (the boats are now in danger) and starts the tension rising as Mr. Reyes struggles in the dark. Because it sets up the danger and leads toward the most intense point rather than settling anything, it belongs to the rising action.

steps: Recall the plot stages: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.
Place the moment in the arc: the lamp failing introduces the central conflict and starts building tension.
Rule out climax: the most intense point is later, when he relights the lamp as a boat nears the rocks.
Rule out resolution: nothing is settled yet. Conclude it is rising action because it sets up the danger and pushes toward the climax.

Read the passage below.

Gabriela had entered the city chess tournament expecting to lose in the first round. Her opponent was last year's champion. For the first twenty moves she played carefully, defensively, just trying not to embarrass herself. Then she noticed her opponent had left a weakness on the board. Her heart pounded. She stopped playing to survive and started playing to win, attacking with a boldness she did not know she had. When her opponent finally tipped over his king, Gabriela realized she had stopped thinking of herself as someone who only hoped not to lose.

Explain how Gabriela's response to noticing the weakness on the board changes the way she plays, and what that reveals about her.
items.answer: When Gabriela notices the weakness on the board, her response is to switch from playing defensively, just trying not to embarrass herself, to attacking boldly to win. The discovery is the trigger: it gives her a reason to take a risk she would not have taken before. This change in how she plays reveals that she has more confidence and ambition in her than she realized. The text shows this when it says she 'started playing to win' with 'a boldness she did not know she had,' and at the end she stops thinking of herself as someone who only hopes not to lose. Her response to the opening on the board reveals a hidden capacity for boldness and self-belief.

steps: Pinpoint the trigger event: Gabriela notices a weakness in her opponent's position.
Describe her response: she shifts from defensive survival play to bold attacking play.
Infer what the response reveals: a hidden confidence and ambition, supported by 'a boldness she did not know she had.'
Tie it to her self-view at the end: she stops seeing herself as someone who only hopes not to lose, confirming the inferred trait.

Read the passage below.

The village sat at the bottom of a steep valley, and every spring the melting snow sent a river rushing through it. For generations the families had built their homes on tall stone stilts to stay above the flood. Young Tomas thought the stilts were old-fashioned and ugly, and he dreamed of a normal house on the ground. But the spring he turned twelve, the snowmelt came early and hard. The river rose higher than anyone remembered, swallowing the lower paths. From his stilted home, dry and safe, Tomas watched the water below and finally understood why his ancestors had built the way they did.

Explain how the setting of the valley shapes both the village's way of life and Tomas's change of mind.
items.answer: The setting, a steep valley that floods every spring from snowmelt, shapes the village's entire way of life: the families build their homes on tall stone stilts to stay above the rising river. This explains a custom that Tomas at first finds old-fashioned and ugly. The setting also drives Tomas's change of mind. When the snowmelt comes early and the river rises higher than anyone remembers, his stilted home keeps him dry and safe. Watching the flood from above, he finally understands why his ancestors built that way. The flood, a feature of the setting, is the event that turns his opinion from dismissal to understanding. The valley both creates the tradition and teaches Tomas its value.

steps: Identify the setting: a steep valley that floods each spring from snowmelt.
Connect the setting to the way of life: the flooding is why homes are built on stilts.
Trace Tomas's starting view and the event that changes it: he scorns the stilts until the early, severe flood.
Explain the change: from his dry, safe home he sees the danger below and understands the tradition, so the setting causes his shift in thinking.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

For years, Mei had let her older brother answer for her. At restaurants he ordered her food. At the doctor he described her symptoms. She found it easier to stay quiet. Then her brother left for college, and Mei went to her first appointment alone. The nurse asked her a question and waited. There was no one to answer for her. Mei's mouth was dry, but she took a breath and spoke for herself, slowly at first, then steadily. Walking home, she realized she had said more in that one hour than she usually said in a week.

Explain how her brother leaving for college functions as the cause of Mei's change, and describe how she is different by the end.
items.answer: Her brother leaving for college is the cause of Mei's change because it removes the person who used to speak for her. For years she stayed quiet and let him order her food and describe her symptoms, which was easier. Once he is gone and she goes to her appointment alone, there is no one to answer for her, so she is forced to speak for herself. By the end, Mei is different: she has found her own voice. She speaks slowly at first, then steadily, and realizes she said more in that hour than she usually says in a week. The change is caused specifically by his absence, which created the situation that made her speak.

steps: Describe Mei at the start: she stays silent and lets her brother speak for her.
Identify the causal event: her brother leaves for college, removing her usual spokesperson.
Explain why that event forces change: alone at the appointment, she has no one to answer for her.
Describe Mei at the end: she speaks steadily for herself and notices she said far more than usual, showing real growth caused by his absence.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The race began, and Ravi shot to the front. He had trained all season and felt certain of the win. At the halfway mark he was still leading, but he heard footsteps gaining behind him. A runner named Soren pulled even, then slightly ahead. Ravi's lungs burned. With fifty meters left, he could see the finish line and Soren's back just in front of him. He dug deeper than he ever had, closing the gap stride by stride, and lunged across the line. The crowd erupted, but Ravi did not yet know who had won.

Identify which stage of the plot the final lunge across the line represents, and explain why.
items.answer: The final lunge across the line represents the climax of the plot. The climax is the moment of greatest tension, the turning point where the central conflict comes to a head. Throughout the passage the conflict has been building: Ravi leads, then Soren pulls ahead, and the gap closes stride by stride. The lunge is the highest point of that rising tension, the instant the race is decided, and it is followed by uncertainty, since Ravi does not yet know who won. Because it is the peak of the conflict and the moment everything has built toward, the lunge is the climax, not the resolution, which would come only when the winner is announced.

steps: Recall that the climax is the peak of tension and the turning point of the conflict.
Trace the rising action: Ravi leads, Soren catches up and passes, the gap closes.
Identify the peak: the final lunge across the line, the most intense moment.
Distinguish it from the resolution: the winner is not yet known, so the outcome is still unsettled. The lunge is the climax.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

When the power went out across the whole neighborhood, the Ortega family lit candles and gathered in the living room. At first the children complained: no television, no video games, no internet. But as the hours passed, they began to talk. Their father told a story about his own childhood that none of them had heard. Their mother taught them a card game from her village. By the time the lights buzzed back on near midnight, the youngest child said, almost disappointed, 'Already?'

Explain how the setting of the blackout leads to a change in the family's evening, and what the youngest child's final word reveals.
items.answer: The setting of the blackout, a power outage with no television, video games, or internet, leads to a change in the family's evening by removing the usual distractions. With nothing electronic to do, the children begin to talk, the father shares a story they had never heard, and the mother teaches a card game. The setting forces a different kind of evening, one based on connection rather than screens. The youngest child's final word, 'Already?', said almost with disappointment when the lights return, reveals that the family has come to enjoy this time together. It shows that the blackout, which seemed like a problem at first, actually gave them something valuable. The setting caused the shift from complaint to closeness.

steps: Identify the setting condition: a blackout that removes screens and electronics.
Trace its effect on the plot: with no devices, the family talks, shares stories, and plays a game.
Interpret the youngest child's word 'Already?': spoken with disappointment, it shows enjoyment of the evening.
Connect setting to change: the blackout caused a shift from complaining to closeness, so the setting drives the plot's emotional turn.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

At the start of the summer, Priya refused to swim in the deep end. She would only wade where she could touch the bottom, watching the older kids dive off the board with envy and fear. Her cousin offered to teach her, but Priya always said no. Then, late in August, a younger child slipped near the deep end and went under. Without thinking, Priya jumped in and pulled the child up, her feet never touching the bottom. Afterward, shaking on the pool deck, she realized she had just swum in the deep end without even noticing.

Describe how Priya changes by the end of the passage, and identify the event that caused the change.
items.answer: At the start, Priya is afraid of the deep end and refuses to swim there, even turning down her cousin's offer to teach her. By the end, she has changed: she has swum in the deep end without even noticing, which shows her fear has been overcome. The event that caused the change is the younger child slipping under the water near the deep end. Without thinking, Priya jumps in to save the child, and in doing so she swims in the very place she had always feared. The emergency, not her cousin's earlier lessons, is the turning point: it pushed her past her fear before she had time to be afraid. The cause is the rescue, and the change is that she has conquered the deep end.

steps: Describe Priya at the start: she fears the deep end and refuses to swim there.
Describe Priya at the end: she has swum in the deep end without noticing, showing her fear is gone.
Locate the turning-point event: the younger child slips under and Priya jumps in to rescue them.
Attribute the change to the correct cause: the emergency, not the earlier offers of lessons, is what pushed her past her fear.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The old farmhouse stood at the end of a long dirt road, miles from the nearest town. When Elena's family inherited it, she dreaded the quiet. There were no streetlights, no traffic, no neighbors within sight. The first night she lay awake, unsettled by how silent and dark it was. But over the weeks, the same setting that had frightened her began to feel different. She learned the night sounds, the owls and crickets. She saw more stars than she had ever seen in the city. By the end of the summer, the quiet that once scared her had become the thing she loved most.

Explain how Elena's relationship to the farmhouse setting changes over the summer, and what causes that change.
items.answer: At the start, Elena dreads the farmhouse setting: its quiet, darkness, and isolation unsettle her, and she lies awake the first night unable to sleep. Over the summer, her relationship to that same setting changes from fear to love. What causes the change is time and growing familiarity. As the weeks pass, she learns the night sounds, the owls and crickets, and she sees more stars than she ever saw in the city. By getting to know the setting rather than just reacting to it, she comes to value what once frightened her. The cause of the change is not a single event but the gradual experience of living in the place, which transforms the quiet from something scary into the thing she loves most.

steps: Describe Elena's first response to the setting: she dreads the dark, silent isolation and cannot sleep.
Trace the change over time: she learns the night sounds and sees the stars.
Identify the cause: gradual familiarity and experience, not a single dramatic event.
State the end point: the quiet she once feared becomes what she loves most, showing the setting reshaped her feelings.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

In the first scene, Coach Bell benched Andre for missing practice, and Andre slammed his locker and shouted that it wasn't fair. In the second scene, Andre sat alone on the bus, replaying his own words and beginning to feel ashamed. In the third scene, he showed up early to the next practice, found the coach, and apologized without being asked. Coach Bell studied him for a moment, then handed him a jersey.

Explain how the second scene connects the first scene to the third, and what this shows about Andre.
items.answer: The second scene connects the first to the third by showing the inner change that makes Andre's apology possible. In the first scene, Andre reacts with anger, slamming his locker and shouting that the benching is unfair. In the second scene, alone on the bus, he replays his own words and begins to feel ashamed. This reflection is the bridge: it turns his anger into regret. In the third scene, that regret leads him to apologize early and without being asked. The middle scene is essential because without it Andre's sudden apology would make no sense. It shows that Andre is capable of self-reflection and growth: he can move from blaming others to taking responsibility once he thinks honestly about his behavior.

steps: Summarize scene one: Andre reacts with anger and blames the coach.
Summarize scene three: Andre apologizes early and without being asked.
Explain the role of scene two: alone on the bus, his shame turns anger into regret, bridging the two.
Draw the trait: Andre is capable of self-reflection and taking responsibility, which the middle scene proves by causing the apology.

Read the passage below.

The carnival arrived in town only once a year, and it always set up in the empty field behind the school. For Lina, that field was ordinary the rest of the year, just a place to cut across on her walk home. But for one week each summer, the same field filled with lights, music, and the smell of fried dough. This year, standing among the booths with her little sister's hand in hers, Lina realized that the magic was not in the field itself. It was in how rare it was, and in who she shared it with. When the carnival packed up and the field went empty again, she found she did not mind. She knew it would return.

Explain how the setting of the field shapes the meaning of the story and Lina's realization.
items.answer: The setting of the field shapes the story's meaning because the very same place is ordinary most of the year, just a shortcut on Lina's walk home, yet becomes magical for one week when the carnival fills it with lights, music, and the smell of fried dough. This contrast is the heart of the story. Standing among the booths with her sister, Lina realizes the magic is not in the field itself but in how rare the carnival is and in who she shares it with. The setting makes this realization possible: only because the field is plain the rest of the year can the carnival week feel special. When the field empties again, Lina does not mind, because she understands that the value comes from rarity and from the people beside her, not from the place alone.

steps: Note the key feature of the setting: the field is ordinary all year but transformed for one carnival week.
Identify the contrast that gives the story meaning: plain shortcut versus magical fairground.
Connect the setting to Lina's realization: the magic comes from rarity and shared company, not the field itself.
Explain why she does not mind the empty field: she now values the experience and the people, which the setting's yearly change taught her.
